P1_fx_receipts.question: Can resident individuals receive foreign currency for services or digital exports? Any conversion or repatriation rule?
P1_fx_receipts.answer: Partly established. Exchange controls exist and are administered by the Central Bank of Eswatini's Exchange Control Department, and all international commercial transactions must go through authorised foreign-exchange dealers (banks). Eswatini is in the Common Monetary Area. Specific rules for residents' foreign service income (surrender, retention, FX accounts) were not captured.
P1_fx_receipts.note: trade.gov guide captured; CBE 'Simple Guide to Exchange Controls' (2022) seen only via third-party mirror in search results, not captured on 2026-10-22.

L1_registration.question: Must an individual register a business to sell digital services/products? Simplest legal form?
L1_registration.answer: Partly established. Businesses start by reserving a name with the Registrar of Companies (reservation SZL 20 per a guide) and then obtain a TIN from the Eswatini Revenue Service. Depending on the activity, a trading licence may be required (Trading Licences Act). A distinct sole-trader procedure was not confirmed.
L1_registration.note: Single commercial guide (Deel) captured, describing company-style steps; Registrar/ERS official pages not captured on 2026-10-22.

L3_income_tax_foreign.question: Income tax on foreign-source income for residents; rates or special regimes
L3_income_tax_foreign.answer: Eswatini taxes on a source basis: income from a source within (or deemed within) the country is taxed, whatever the recipient's residence. Rates are progressive (20% on the first SZL 100,000, rising above that). Whether remote work done in Eswatini for foreign clients is local-source was not confirmed.

sources.title: Eswatini - Individual - Taxes on personal income
sources.quote: Income tax is levied on all income derived from a source within or deemed to be within the country, irrespective of whether the recipient of the income is actually resident in Eswatini.

L4_vat_gst.question: VAT/GST: rate, registration threshold, treatment of exported digital services
L4_vat_gst.answer: VAT is 15% (PwC, reviewed March 2026), introduced in 2012 at 14%. The registration threshold has been E500,000 since 2012; a 2025 study recommended raising it to E900,000, but no amendment was found. A 2026 VAT Amendment Bill on non-resident electronic-service suppliers and e-invoicing was awaiting assent in October 2026.

L5_data_protection.answer: The Data Protection Act (2022) establishes a Commission with power to impose administrative fines and requires breach notification. W1_workarounds.question: Simple, legal routes around payment barriers for a beginner (no misrepresentation, nominees or sanctions evasion)
W1_workarounds.answer: Barriers: Stripe does not accept merchants here; platforms that pay out through PayPal Payouts cannot pay PayPal accounts here (not on PayPal's Payouts list, see P4 for ordinary PayPal receiving); Wise does not let residents hold money. Simple legal routes: (1) Sell digital products or software through a merchant of record: Paddle (software/SaaS only; each seller reviewed), Dodo Payments. The platform is the legal seller to your customers, handles card payments and consumer VAT/sales tax, and pays you out. You still declare the payouts as your income at home (see L3). (2) Sell services on Upwork, which is available here (not on its restricted list). Which withdrawal methods you get (bank, PayPal, Payoneer, etc.) depends on the country and shows in your account. (3) Paid apps and in-app sales through Google Play (merchant registration available here). (4) For direct clients, a bank transfer (SWIFT) into your own local account always works. Follow the local foreign-exchange rules (see P1) and keep invoices. Avoid: opening accounts with a foreign address, a relative's or friend's identity, or a VPN to look like you are elsewhere. It breaches platform terms (accounts and funds get frozen) and can break anti-money-laundering or sanctions law.
